specPoints.text: know the definition of the term 'half-life' and understand that it is different for different radioactive isotopes
use the concept of the half-life to carry out simple calculations on activity, including graphical methods

primer.text: No clock can time a single nucleus, but a sample keeps a timetable: the half-life. It is the time for the activity — or the nuclei count — to halve, it is fixed for each isotope, and it spans from fractions of a second to billions of years. Graphs turn it into easy arithmetic.

lessons.title: Defining half-life
lessons.opening: Half-life is the time needed for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample — equivalently the activity — to fall to half its starting value. Each isotope has its own fixed half-life, and measuring one is simply timing the fall from an initial activity to half of it.
keyPoints: Half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei to halve.
Equivalently, it is the time for the activity to fall to half its initial value.
Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years.
Measure the initial activity, then time the fall to half of that value.

low.restatement: Watch the meter: 800, 400, 200, 100… the gaps between halvings are all the same length — that gap is the half-life.
low.analogy: Half-life is like a queue leaving a stadium at a steady pattern — every ten minutes, half of whoever remains walks out.
low.examPointer: Both phrasings score: "number of nuclei halves" or "activity halves". Tie them together for full credit.

medium.restatement: Because decay probability per nucleus is constant, any fixed fraction of the remaining nuclei decays per unit time; the half is just the most convenient fraction, and halving repeats indefinitely — never quite reaching zero. Isotope identity fixes the probability, hence the half-life.
medium.analogy: A photocopier set to 50%: each copy is half the previous one, forever approaching but never hitting blank.
medium.examPointer: Half-life never "runs out" — after n half-lives, (1/2)ⁿ remains. Quote the table 100-50-25-12.5-6.25%.

check.stem: Which statement correctly defines the half-life of a sample of unstable nuclei?

options.text: the time for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve
the time for a sample to become completely stable
the time for one particular nucleus to decay
the average lifetime of a detector

check.stem: After two half-lives, what fraction of the original unstable nuclei remains?

options.explanation: Half of a half is a quarter.
Halving approaches zero but never reaches it.

check.stem: Why can a single nucleus’s decay moment never be found, even though a sample’s half-life is measurable?

options.text: because decay is random per nucleus, but large samples show a steady statistical pattern

options.explanation: There is no literal hiding — it is statistics.

options.text: because half-life depends on the detector
options.explanation: Half-life is a property of the isotope.

check.stem: The half-life of carbon-14 is 5700 years, while uranium-235 needs 704 million years. This comparison shows…

options.explanation: The two isotopes span enormous ranges.

options.text: carbon always decays faster than every element

options.explanation: Half-life is independent of sample size.
Activity depends on the sample, not just the isotope.

check.stem: A sample’s activity falls from 600 Bq to 300 Bq in 8 days. Its half-life is…

options.explanation: The activity halved exactly once in 8 days.
That would be the half-life if it had halved twice.
That doubles the elapsed time with no reason.

check.modelAnswer: Half-life is the time needed for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample — equivalently, the activity — to fall to half its starting value.

check.stem: State the range of half-life values isotopes can have.
check.modelAnswer: Half-lives span enormous ranges — a fraction of a second at one extreme, billions of years at the other — and each isotope has its own fixed value.

check.stem: Explain why the half-life of an isotope is constant regardless of how old the sample is.
check.modelAnswer: Each nucleus has a fixed decay probability per unit time set by the isotope itself; the remaining nuclei therefore always halve in the same time, however long the sample has existed.

check.stem: An isotope’s initial activity is 720 Bq. State the activity after three half-lives.

lessons.title: Half-life calculations
sourceHeadings: A graph can be used to make half-life calculations
lessons.opening: Half-life arithmetic runs on repeated halving: divide the activity by 2 per half-life, or count halvings between two activities and divide the elapsed time by that count. On a graph, read the initial activity, find half of it, and read off the time — constant per isotope.
keyPoints: Each half-life halves the remaining activity or nuclei count.
Number of half-lives = elapsed time ÷ half-life.
On an activity-time graph, the half-life is the time to fall from any value to half of it.
The half-life read between 100%→50% equals that from 50%→25%.
A sample falling 880 → 440 → 220 Bq in one year has a half-life of 6 months.

low.restatement: Start 880 Bq: after one half-life 440, after two 220. Two halvings took a year, so one half-life is six months.
low.analogy: Keep halving a pizza: every cut takes the same time, and counting cuts tells you the kitchen’s rhythm.
low.examPointer: Write the halving chain explicitly (880 → 440 → 220) — the visible chain is the working examiners reward.

medium.restatement: Graphically, choose a clean starting value A₀, locate A₀/2 on the axis, and read the horizontal gap; the same gap recurs for A₀/2→A₀/4, which is the consistency check. Arithmetic-wise, converting elapsed time into half-life counts (n = t/T½) and applying (1/2)ⁿ to the initial activity solves both directions.
medium.analogy: Reading a half-life graph is like using a repeated staircase: every riser is the same height (the half) and the same tread (the half-life).
medium.examPointer: Technetium-style graph questions: draw the horizontal lines at A₀ and A₀/2 on the printed figure — visible construction earns method marks.

check.stem: A sample’s activity drops from 880 Bq to 220 Bq in one year. How many half-lives passed?
Using the previous halving chain, the half-life of that sample is…

options.explanation: A year holds two half-lives here.
That would fit four half-lives per year.
The half-life must be shorter than the elapsed year.

check.stem: On an activity-time graph, the half-life is found by…

options.text: reading the time for the activity to fall from its starting value to half of it
reading where the curve touches zero
taking the total time shown on the axis

options.explanation: Gradients are not part of the method.

check.stem: An isotope has a half-life of 8 hours. Starting from 640 Bq, the activity after 24 hours is…
For carbon-14 the half-life is 5700 years. After 11 400 years, the fraction of carbon-14 remaining is…
State the two-step method to find a half-life from an activity-time graph.
check.modelAnswer: Read the initial activity A₀, locate A₀/2 on the activity axis, and read the time at which the curve reaches it — that time is the half-life.

check.stem: A sample falls from 880 Bq to 220 Bq in one year. State the number of half-lives and the half-life.
check.modelAnswer: Two half-lives passed (880 → 440 → 220), so the half-life is 6 months.

check.stem: Explain why the time taken to fall from 50% to 25% of the initial activity equals the time from 100% to 50%.
check.modelAnswer: Halving is proportional, not absolute: the isotope’s fixed half-life halves whatever amount is present, so each successive halving takes the same time.

check.stem: A technetium sample’s activity falls from 8 × 10⁷ Bq to 4 × 10⁷ Bq in 6 hours. State its half-life and its activity after 12 hours.
check.modelAnswer: The half-life is 6 hours (the fall to half A₀); after 12 hours (two half-lives) the activity is 2 × 10⁷ Bq.

glossary.definition: The time for the number of unstable nuclei, or the activity, of a sample to halve.
The activity of a sample at the start of the measurement (A₀).
Finding the half-life by reading the time for the curve to fall from A₀ to A₀/2.

workedExample.prompt: The activity of a radioactive sample is 880 Bq. After one year it has dropped to 220 Bq. What is the half-life of this material?
steps: Two half-lives elapsed in one year.
